extracted.intended_audience: experimental chemists, natural philosophers, members of learned societies and students of chemistry
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for conducting, reporting, and organizing experimental chemical research and for writing an elementary treatise of chemistry: emphasis on measurement, apparatus, nomenclature, ordering of material, and restraint from speculation beyond experimental facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit conclusions to experimental evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ne rien conclure au-delà de ce que les expériences présentent; 'se proposer de ne rien conclure au-delà de ce que les expériences présentent & de ne jamais suppléer au silence des faits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not advance generalities or speculative doctrines unless supported by rigorous experiments; avoid filling gaps with conjecture. The author repeatedly insists the treatise should only state what experiments provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise nomenclature linking words to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity and advantage of 'lier les mots aux faits' and a methodical nomenclature that makes names exact and useful to progress in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a systematic, unambiguous naming scheme (e.g., names reflecting composition or proportion of oxygen). Precise language prevents false ideas and aids scientific progress; the treatise emphasizes the influence of exact names on study and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement and weighing as fundamental method
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish opinions 'la balance à la main' — experiments must be rigourous and based on weighing and quantitative measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh reactants and products, record masses precisely, and base reasoning on these quantitative results. The reviewer stresses that modern discoveries arose from 'tout recueillir, à tout peser.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe apparatus and manual operations with indispensable detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a 'description sommaire de tous les appareils & de toutes les opérations manuelles' with the 'détails indispensables' necessary for use and replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient procedural detail so that the reader can reproduce operations; reserve lengthy technical descriptions to avoid interrupting conceptual exposition, but do provide them (often in a separate, detailed section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent and use specialized apparatus to reveal causes and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and employ new instruments for effervescences, combustions, calcination, gasometry, calorimetry, distillations pneumato-chimiques, &c.; many such instruments are due to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop apparatus specifically tailored to isolate variables and make causes/results visible (examples: devices for measuring gas volumes and weights; ice-envelope calorimeter). Carefully describe and illustrate such instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize presentation from simple elements to complex combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduce readers 'en partant des notions les plus simples & des objets les plus élémentaires' successively to more complex combinations; the treatise is divided into elements, combinations, and apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure exposition so beginners progress from fundamental principles to compound subjects; use an ordered sequence (e.g., elements → their combinations → apparatus) to aid comprehension and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from treating chemical affinities generally until data are precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include general discussions of 'affinités ou attractions chimiques' when the principal data are 'ni assez précises, ni assez certaines' to support such generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold off on broad theoretical generalizations about affinities until sufficient precise, reproducible data exist; if others are preparing the topic (e.g., competing treatments), avoid premature competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative reference tables and conversion data
rubrics_metrics.description: Include practical tables: cubic inches to weight of water, conversions between vulgar and decimal fractions, weights of different gases, specific gravities of substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply compact reference material to support experimental work and conversions; tables should be accurate and facilitate calculations in the laboratory and in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure calorific changes quantitatively (ice-calorimetry example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an ice calorimeter (envelopes of tôle garnies de glace) to measure calorique produced during fixation of 'air vital' and combustion; e.g., melting of precise weights of ice corresponds to heat released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify heat evolved or absorbed using controlled calorimetric apparatus; design experiments to convert thermal output into a measurable physical change (melting ice) and report masses and conversions clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform mass-balance/stoichiometric accounting in chemical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for masses in reactions (examples: 100 grains of phosphore absorb 154 grains of air base to form 254 grains of acid; water composition experiments balancing O and H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and report how much of each substance is consumed and produced; use these balances to deduce composition (e.g., composition of water, formation of acids) and to support nomenclature and theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze gaseous mixtures and quantify component proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose and measure atmosphere: demonstrate air is a compound of two elastic fluids, one respirable (0.27) and one non-respirable (0.73).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate and weigh/measure gas fractions, report proportions quantitatively, and use multiple experimental approaches to confirm composition of mixtures like air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt nomenclature reflecting oxygen proportions (acids vs. oxides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Call a substance 'acide' when combination with oxygen gives acidic character; term 'oxide' for substances not sufficiently oxygeneated to be acids; vary terminations to indicate degree of oxygenation (sulfurous vs sulfuric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic naming rules that encode composition (amount of oxygen) and thus clarify relationships between related compounds; explain the principles of the nomenclature in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include carefully engraved plates and visual details of instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Accompany apparatus descriptions with numerous plates 'gravées avec beaucoup de soin' that present all desired details; illustrations are essential for making descriptions sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide high-quality figures that show construction and detail of experimental setups so practitioners can accurately reproduce instruments and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate findings with independent experiments and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare and show agreement with experiments of other investigators (Bergman, Scheele, Cavendish, Priestley, etc.); mutual confirmation strengthens the doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and compare independent experimental results; seek concordance across different methods and investigators to increase confidence in conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'elements' as the terminal results of analysis, not speculative simples
rubrics_metrics.description: Regard what are called elements as the last results of analysis ('les derniers résultats que nous en obtenons') rather than hypothesized indivisible molecules; avoid asserting speculative atomic claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define elements operationally—substances obtained as ultimate products of analysis—and avoid extending beyond experimentally established composition when discussing elemental theory.
